new-york.blurb: New York City's courts are organized by borough, and each borough is its own county. In Manhattan, the Supreme Court of the State of New York, New York County, is the main trial court for civil cases of any size, with its principal courthouse at 60 Centre Street. The Civil Court of the City of New York hears smaller civil matters, and its Small Claims Part takes claims up to $10,000 without a lawyer; the Manhattan branch is at 111 Centre Street. Federal cases from Manhattan and the Bronx go to the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, while Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island fall within the Eastern District of New York, based at 225 Cadman Plaza East in Brooklyn. Immigration cases are heard at several EOIR courts in Manhattan, including 26 Federal Plaza. Lawyers' registration status can be checked through the New York State Unified Court System's attorney search.

The court's Small Claims Division handles civil claims of $12,500 or less, with simplified rules and no lawyers at the hearing. Federal cases go to the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, whose Los Angeles courthouses include the Felicitas and Gonzalo Mendez United States Courthouse at 350 W. 1st Street and the Edward R. chicago.blurb: The Circuit Court of Cook County is the state trial court for Chicago, handling civil, criminal, family and other cases. Its First Municipal District covers the city, and its main civil courthouse is the Richard J. Daley Center at 50 W. Washington St., which also hosts small claims. Illinois small claims cases cover money claims up to $10,000, and a pro se small claims track at the Daley Center is reserved for self-represented parties with claims up to $3,000. Felony cases in the city are heard at the George N. Leighton Criminal Courthouse. Federal cases go to the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, Eastern Division, at the Dirksen United States Courthouse on South Dearborn Street. Immigration cases are heard at the Chicago Immigration Court on East Monroe Street. Illinois lawyers' licenses and discipline records can be checked through the Attorney Registration and Disciplinary Commission (ARDC).

Smaller civil disputes and small claims go to the county's Justice of the Peace courts, which also hear Class C misdemeanors. Federal cases go to the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas, Houston Division, at the Bob Casey United States Courthouse on Rusk Street. Houston has more than one EOIR immigration court, including one at 500 Jefferson Street. The Houston Lawyer Referral Service, affiliated with the Houston Bar Association, is certified under Texas law. Lawyers' licenses can be verified through the State Bar of Texas.

The Municipal Court's Civil Division hears landlord-tenant cases, code enforcement cases, and small claims up to $12,000; larger claims go to the Court of Common Pleas. Federal cases go to the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania at the James A. Byrne U.S. Courthouse, 601 Market Street. The Philadelphia Immigration Court is in the Robert Nix Federal Building at 900 Market Street. Small claims, part of the district court, are decided by magistrates, and North Carolina counties set limits between $5,000 and $10,000. Charlotte is also one of four locations of the North Carolina Business Court, which handles complex business cases. Federal cases are filed in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of North Carolina at 401 West Trade Street, with appeals to the Fourth Circuit. EOIR's Charlotte Immigration Court is at 5701 Executive Center Drive. Denver County Court, which functions as both a municipal and a state court, handles misdemeanors, traffic matters, civil claims up to $25,000 and small claims up to $7,500. Federal cases go to the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado at the Alfred A. Arraj U.S. Courthouse, and the Denver Immigration Court sits on Stout Street.
